    Lesson 1 · 30 minutes

    Context and memory: what your assistant can actually see

    By the end of this lesson you can decide, for each piece of information in your makerspace assistant, whether it stays in the context, gets saved for later, or gets looked up when needed, and say why.

    Objective O3: context and memory in an agentAbout 30 minutes
    Why this matters for you

    Your assistant has to answer from long machine manuals and remember each student's training status between visits. You also have a small model budget. All three come down to one design question: what goes into each model call?

    In this lesson
    1. Warm-up
    2. The context window
    3. Between steps
    4. When the context gets crowded
    5. Between sessions, and notes as memory
    6. Retrieval
    7. Worked example and practice
    8. Summary

    Warm-up 2 min

    Answer from memory before you open each answer. Pulling an idea back out helps it stick.

    {reveal("Recall 1","A chatbot confidently gives last year's makerspace opening hours. Using what you know about language models, why can that happen?","

    The model has what it learned in training plus the text it is given. If current hours are in neither, it can still produce a believable sentence that is out of date. Today is about controlling the second source: the text it is given.

    ")} {reveal("Recall 2","A student asks, “Is the 3D printer free Monday?” Sketch the agent loop for this request, from question to stop.","

    The model gets the goal and the available tools. It asks for a calendar lookup. The program carries it out. The result goes back to the model. The model either asks for another action or gives a final answer. A limit can also end the loop. Today's question: at each of those turns, what is in front of the model?

    ")}

    The context window 4 min

    Start with an example. A student types, “Can I cut this plywood on the laser cutter?” Your program does not send only that sentence. It also sends the assistant's rules, the descriptions of its tools, and any earlier messages. It might add a page from the manual too.

    All of that text is the context: what the model is given to work from on this call. Anthropic's engineers describe it as the set of tokens included when the model generates output ({a(CE,"context engineering article")}).

    A token is a small unit of text that a model reads and writes. It can be a word, part of a word, a character, or even bytes ({a(GL,"glossary")}). So a token count is not a word count. Different models split text differently. When you need a real number, use your model provider's token counter or the usage figures returned with each reply.

    The context window is the limit on how much text the model can work with at once. One provider's documentation describes it as all the text the model can reference when generating a response, including the response itself, and calls it the model's working memory ({a(CW,"context windows documentation")}).

    The same page says what counts: the system prompt, every message, tool results, images, documents, and tool definitions. The reply counts too. A system prompt is the standing set of instructions your program sends, such as “You help students at the makerspace.”

    {fig1}

    Think of a workbench with a fixed area. The drawings, the manual, your parts, and the space where you assemble all share it. A thick binder on the bench leaves less room for everything else.

    How big is the window? It depends on the model. At the time I checked the documentation, it listed windows of 200,000 and 1 million tokens for different models ({a(CW,"source")}). Check the figure for whatever model your team picks.

    What if you go over? It depends on the API and model. In the documentation above, input that is too large by itself is rejected with an error. A reply that runs into the limit can be cut off, and on some models a request that asks for too much reply room is rejected up front ({a(CW,"details")}). Don't assume the model will quietly make room. Your program has to manage the space.

    {mis("“The context window is everything the model knows.” It is tempting because both feel like the model's knowledge. But training is what the model learned before you called it. The window holds the text for the current work. Your makerspace's new laser cutter rule does not enter training just because you put it in a prompt. It is available while it is in the context.")} {check("Your team adds ten long tool descriptions. No student has typed anything yet. What happens to the window?",[ ("They use space on each call that includes them",True,"Tool definitions are part of the input, so they take room even if no tool is ever used."), ("They use space only after a tool is called",False,"The model has to see a description to decide whether to call the tool, so it is there before any call. This applies to definitions sent up front."), ("They use no space because they aren't messages",False,"The window is not just chat messages. Tool definitions count too.")], "Definitions sent with a call take up space on that call, whether or not a tool gets used. Short, clear descriptions help your budget.")}

    Between steps: the program carries the history 6 min

    Here is the surprise for many new builders. The model API in the documentation I used is stateless: it keeps nothing from your last call for the next one. To continue a conversation, you send the whole history again ({a(WM,"working with messages")}). An API is the interface your Python code calls, like the web API in your class project.

    Some services offer to store the history for you. Even then, ask what is being put in front of the model on each call. In this lesson, assume your own program keeps the history.

    In Python terms, picture a list. Your program appends each new item and passes the list on the next call. This is a sketch, not a real library:

    history = [question]
while steps < MAX_STEPS:
    reply = call_model(rules, tools, history)
    history.append(reply)
    if reply.is_final_answer:
        break
    result = run_tool(reply)      # your program runs it
    history.append(result)
    steps += 1

    Each time around the loop is a separate model call. The model can use the calendar result in the next step because your program put it into history and sent it. If you delete history.append(result), the next call has no idea what the calendar said.

    So “what is kept between steps” has a plain answer: whatever your program keeps and sends again. This within-one-conversation history is often called short-term memory. One agent framework defines it as memory scoped to a single thread, meaning one conversation. Its saved state also lets that thread be resumed later ({a(LG,"memory overview")}).

    Why this costs money

    Worked example: counting one request

    A student asks, “Is the laser cutter free Friday, and what plywood can it cut?” These sizes are made up to keep the arithmetic easy.

    • Rules and tool definitions: 1,500 tokens
    • Question: 50 tokens
    • Each tool request the model writes: 50 tokens
    • Calendar result: 300 tokens
    • Manual search result: 2,000 tokens
    • Final answer: 200 tokens
    1. Call 1 reads 1,500 + 50 = 1,550. The model asks for the calendar.
    2. Call 2 reads the old 1,550, plus the 50-token request, plus the 300-token result: 1,900. The model asks for a manual search.
    3. Call 3 reads 1,900 + 50 + 2,000 = 3,950. The model writes the 200-token answer.
    4. Total input: 1,550 + 1,900 + 3,950 = 7,400 tokens. Total output: 50 + 50 + 200 = 300.
    5. Space used by the end: 3,950 + 200 = 4,150.
    {bars()}

    Notice two different numbers. The window question is about one call: does this call fit? The cost question adds up all the calls. The 1,500 tokens of rules and tools were sent three times.

    If the student then asks a follow-up in the same chat, and you keep everything, the next call starts with those 4,150 tokens plus the new question. The documentation describes this build-up: each turn's messages accumulate in the window ({a(CW,"source")}). A turn here means a user message and the assistant's response.

    Some providers offer prompt caching, which can change the price of repeated input. Cached text still takes up room in the window ({a(CW,"source")}). The totals here count tokens, not dollars. Some models also produce “thinking” tokens, with their own rules about what is carried forward. I leave them out here.

    Call 1: 1,000 + 100 = 1,100. Call 2: 1,100 + 50 + 600 = 1,750. Total input: 2,850. The result is not the only thing call 2 reads. It also rereads everything from call 1 and the request.

    ","Show a solution")}

    When the context gets crowded 4 min

    Picture a student who spends an hour troubleshooting a 3D printer with your assistant. Forty messages and many tool results pile up. Most of the old printer status readings no longer matter.

    Running out of room is one problem. Quality is another. As the token count grows, the model's ability to accurately recall information from the context can drop. This is called context rot ({a(CE,"engineering article")}; {a(CW,"documentation")}). The article describes a gradual decline, not a sudden cliff. So aim for a context with the right information, not the most.

    Your program has several ways to tidy up:

    MoveWhat it doesRisk
    Clear old tool resultsDrops bulky results that are no longer neededYou may need one again
    Trim old messagesRemoves earlier parts of the historyAn early detail disappears
    CompactionSummarizes the history and continues from the summaryThe summary leaves something out

    Compaction means taking a conversation that is nearing the window limit, summarizing it, and starting a fresh context with that summary ({a(CE,"source")}). The same article warns that compacting too aggressively can lose details whose importance only shows up later. It also describes clearing tool results as a light form of this.

    For the printer chat, a useful summary might say: “Prints lift at one corner. Bed was cleaned and releveled. Problem remains. Next: check bed temperature.” It keeps decisions and open problems, and drops forty raw readings.

    Compaction is not free: if a model writes the summary, that is model work you pay for. A short chat may never need it. Also, removing something from the context is not the same as deleting it from your database. Your program can keep the full record and send only part of it.

    {check("A long chat is compacted. The summary omits the student's material, and no other copy is sent. What now?",[ ("The model still remembers it from earlier calls",False,"Earlier calls leave nothing behind in a stateless setup. Only what is sent now is available from the conversation."), ("The model cannot rely on it this call",True,"It is not in the context. The model might guess, so your program should let it ask the student or look up a saved copy."), ("The model automatically reopens the old full history",False,"Nothing reopens by itself. Your program would need to fetch the history, or give the model a tool that does.")], "The model can't rely on a detail that is no longer in front of it. It may still guess, which is risky for material safety. Keep must-not-lose facts somewhere your program can reliably reload.")}

    Between sessions, and notes as memory 6 min

    On Monday a student says, “I'm building a plywood enclosure for my sensor project.” On Thursday they open a new chat and ask, “What settings should I look up for my project?” For the assistant to know what “my project” is, something from Monday has to reach Thursday's context.

    Long-term memory is information kept across separate conversations or sessions ({a(LG,"memory overview")}). A session here means one visit or chat. In the design we're discussing, the information lives outside the model, in storage your system controls.

    {fig3} {mis("“The assistant will just remember its users.” It is tempting because some chat apps appear to remember you. When an app does that, something in the system around the model is supplying the information. In your own build, you have to design it: what gets saved, where, who it belongs to, and when it is loaded. Calling the same model again does not do this for you.")}

    Notes the agent writes

    Structured note-taking, also called agentic memory, means the agent regularly writes notes to storage outside the context window and pulls them back in later ({a(CE,"engineering article")}). A to-do list or a NOTES.md file are examples from that article.

    For your assistant, the model might ask to use a save_note tool. Your program runs it and stores the text. Later, the program either loads the note at the start or offers a read_notes tool. Either way, the note helps only once its text is in the context.

    Notes also help within a long task. If the printer troubleshooting history gets compacted or reset, a short note of “already tried” steps can be read back. That saves repeating them.

    Not every saved fact is a “note”

    This next part is my design advice for your project. Sort saved information by how much it matters that it is exactly right.

    InformationWhere it should liveHow it reaches the model
    Training statusThe official training recordsA tool looks it up for the signed-in student
    BookingsThe booking calendarA tool checks it when needed
    Project details, preferencesPer-student notesLoaded or searched when relevant
    Old chat transcriptsA log, only if you need and may keep itNot sent by default

    Why not save “trained on laser cutter” as a model-written note? The model could misread a sentence like “I'm getting trained Friday.” The note could also go stale if training expires. The official record is the thing to trust. Your program should also enforce training rules when booking, not leave that only to the model.

    For notes, decide four things:

    • What to save: facts likely to help later, not every sentence.
    • Whose it is: tie it to the signed-in account, so one student's notes never load for another. Don't let the model pick the ID.
    • How old it is: store a date. Update or remove notes that stop being true.
    • Who can fix it: students should have a way to see and correct what is stored. Check your university's privacy rules.
    {check("Last month's note says a student prefers PLA filament. Today they say they use PETG. What should happen?",[ ("Keep the old note, since saved facts win",False,"Saving something does not make it true forever. Preferences change."), ("Use today's statement, and update the note",True,"The newer, direct statement beats the old note for a preference. Updating stops the stale fact from returning next visit."), ("Store both notes, without dates or labels",False,"A later call could load two conflicting facts with no way to tell which is current.")], "Use what the student just said and update the dated note. This is for preferences. A student's claim should not overwrite an official training record.")}

    Retrieval: finding the right page 5 min

    Suppose the laser cutter manual is 100,000 tokens (again, a made-up size). A student asks how to clean the lens. You could paste the whole manual into the context. In a three-call request that keeps it throughout, that is 300,000 input tokens for the manual alone. Even if it fits the window, you pay in cost and risk context rot.

    A librarian doesn't read you the whole library. They fetch the useful pages. Retrieval means searching a store of information and bringing back the relevant parts. When those parts are given to the model to help it answer, the method is called retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG ({a(CR,"contextual retrieval article")}).

    {fig4}

    A chunk is a short piece of a document. The article above describes chunks of usually no more than a few hundred tokens ({a(CR,"source")}). That is a starting point to test, not a law.

    There are two common ways to search:

    • Keyword search matches words and phrases. A widely used scoring method is called BM25. It is strong for exact strings such as a part number ({a(CR,"source")}).
    • Meaning-based search uses embeddings: lists of numbers that represent the meaning of text. The question and chunks are embedded with the same model, then the closest chunks are found ({a(MS,"Microsoft's guide")}). This can match “the beam looks weak” with a passage on “low output power.”

    Embedding search can miss an important exact match, so some systems combine both ({a(CR,"source")}). For a first version, simple keyword search over well-labeled chunks is a reasonable thing to try. Test it with real student questions.

    Where retrieval goes wrong

    Imagine a chunk that says only, “Replace it every 200 hours.” Replace what, on which machine? Splitting can strip away the context a passage needs ({a(CR,"source")}). Keep the machine name, manual section, and page number with each chunk. The article's own technique goes further and adds a short explanation of where each chunk fits before indexing it.

    Search can also return a similar but wrong passage, or miss the right one. The model sees only what came back from the manual search. Have the assistant name the page it used, and say when the passages don't answer the question. For safety questions, point the student to makerspace staff. These steps reduce risk but don't guarantee a correct answer.

    When does search happen? Your program can search before calling the model. Or the model can request a search tool when it needs one. The second is one form of just-in-time retrieval: the agent keeps pointers such as file paths or links and loads data while it works ({a(CE,"source")}). It can keep unneeded text out, but looking things up at run time takes longer than using material fetched ahead. In your loop, a model-requested search also adds a model call. A mix is possible: always include a few essential rules, and look up everything else.

    Retrieval and memory fit together. Both keep information outside the window and bring in some of it. You can retrieve from manuals or from a large set of saved notes. Retrieved text stays in later calls for as long as your program keeps it in the history.

    {check("A student types an exact replacement part code from a label. Which search is the safer bet?",[ ("Meaning search alone, comparing the overall topic",False,"A code carries little everyday meaning, and embedding search can miss exact matches."), ("Keyword search, matching that exact code string",True,"Exact strings are where keyword search is strong. This assumes the manual's text contains the code and your indexing keeps it intact."), ("No search, relying on the model's training",False,"The model may not know your machine's parts, and could produce a believable wrong answer.")], "Keyword search is the safer bet for an exact code. Meaning search helps when students describe a problem in their own words.")}

    Worked example and practice 4 min

    Worked example: planning one request

    A returning student asks, “Book me the laser cutter Friday at 2, and remind me how to focus it.”

    1. Always send: the rules, the tool definitions, and this request. The model needs them to act.
    2. Load from memory: only notes that could matter, found using the signed-in account. A filament preference can stay out.
    3. Look up exact records: training status from the official records and availability from the calendar. Both can change, so check now.
    4. Retrieve: the few manual chunks on focusing this laser cutter, with page numbers. Leave the rest of the manual out.
    5. Carry between steps: your program adds each tool request and result to the history it sends next.
    6. Save afterwards: the booking goes in the calendar through the booking tool. Save a note only if something useful for later came up. Bulky manual chunks don't need to be copied into memory, since you can retrieve them again.
    Your turn

    A student has spent 30 messages fixing a failing 3D print. They say, “I have to go. Let's continue next week.” Decide: (1) What should be saved? (2) What should not be loaded next week? (3) What has to be checked fresh? (4) How will you find help in the printer manual? Write one line for each. The first is started for you: “Save a dated note, tied to this account, containing …”

    Show a solution
    1. The printer, the symptom, what was tried and what happened, and the next step to try.
    2. By default, not all 30 messages or every old status reading. Load the short note. Keep a full log only if there is a reason and you are allowed to.
    3. Anything that can change, such as printer availability, training status, and the machine's current state.
    4. Search the manual using the symptom and printer model. Bring back a few labeled chunks. Use exact keyword matching for any error text.

    Check yours: could a new session carry on from your note without rereading the chat? Did you avoid treating an old reading as current?

    Defend it at design review

    A teammate says, “Our model has a huge window. Let's send every manual and every old chat each time.” Reply in two or three sentences.

    Show one good reply

    “Even if it fits, we would pay for that input on repeated calls, and a crowded context can make recall worse. Old chats also bring stale or unrelated details, and could expose other students' information. Let's send what this request needs, look up the rest, and measure token use and answer quality on real questions.”

    Summary 1 min

    • The context window is limited space shared by everything the model reads and the reply it writes.
    • Between steps, your program keeps the history and sends it again. Repeated input adds up.
    • A crowded context can hurt recall. Clearing, trimming, and compaction save space but can lose details.
    • Between sessions, information must be stored outside the model and put back into context. Use official records for facts like training.
    • Retrieval brings in selected passages. It can miss, so label sources and check results.

    Say it in your own words: without looking, explain to a teammate how something a student said on Monday could affect an answer on Thursday. Name every step.

    Go further

    Read next: {a(CE,"Effective context engineering for AI agents")}. It is the best single follow-up here because it connects context rot, compaction, note-taking, and just-in-time retrieval. It also discusses splitting work across several agents, which you can save for later. It comes from a model provider, so treat product details as that provider's.

    • {a(CW,"Context windows")}: what counts toward one provider's window.
    • {a(WM,"Working with messages")}: sending conversation history in API calls.
    • {a(CR,"Introducing contextual retrieval")}: chunks, keyword and embedding search, and lost context.
    • {a(LG,"Memory overview")}: short-term and long-term memory in one framework.

    Test it with others: your design review is the first place. You could also look at r/AI_Agents (here is a {a(COM,"directory listing")}; I haven't checked the forum's quality myself). Share your table of what is sent, saved, and looked up, and ask what could fail. Leave out student data.

I wrote your 30-minute lesson on context and memory: [`lessons/0001-context-and-memory.html`](lessons/0001-context-and-memory.html). Open it in your browser. By the end, you should be able to decide what your makerspace assistant keeps in context, saves for later or looks up, and explain why.

It covers:
- **Context window:** what tokens are, and what takes up space.
- **Between steps:** your program sends the history again on each call. A worked token count shows why that matters for your budget.
- **Crowded context:** why recall can get worse, and the risks of clearing, trimming or summarizing old material.
- **Between sessions:** notes as memory, and why training status should come from the official records rather than a note the model wrote.
- **Retrieval:** finding the right parts of a long manual, and how that search can fail.

It also has practice questions, including a design-review challenge. I added a [cheat sheet](cheatsheets/context-and-memory.html) and listed the sources in `RESOURCES.md`.

**Checking the facts:** The main source is [Anthropic's article on context engineering](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents). I read it and most other technical sources through a page-reading helper that sent back summaries and short quotes. For the point that the API keeps nothing between calls, I relied on search results about [the messages guide](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/working-with-messages) and didn't open the page. The token counts and manual size are made up for the examples. The advice on training records and notes is my own design recommendation. Window sizes and API behavior vary, so check them for the model your team chooses.

**Length:** The section times add up to 30 minutes. My command to count the words and check that the quiz files are valid JSON needed approval and didn't run, so neither is verified. I also haven't previewed the lesson in a browser.

Quiz 0002 has five questions and is ready when you are; it works well after a short break. Your two attempts at quiz 0001 haven't been graded yet. I suggest having me grade them next, to check some agent-loop ideas that this lesson builds on. You can also ask me about anything in the lesson.
